items.prompt: The notes bounced around the hall like rain on a tin roof. Why did the writer choose this simile?

options.text: to show that it was raining outside
options.why: There is no real rain. The notes only sounded like rain.

options.text: to show that the music was quick, bright and lively
to show that the hall had a tin roof
options.why: The simile is about the sound, not the building.

options.text: to show that the music was sad
options.why: Rain on a tin roof is a lively pattering sound, not a sad one.

hints: Think about the sound of rain on a tin roof.
Is it slow or quick? Soft or bright?
Now think about many angklung notes being played one after another.
items.explanation: Rain on a tin roof makes lots of quick, bright tapping sounds. The simile helps us hear how lively the angklung music was.

items.prompt: Why does the letter use the words Firstly, Secondly and Finally?

options.text: to list the things they need for the cake sale
options.why: These words introduce reasons for the refill station.

options.text: to show what time each lesson starts
options.why: These words are not about time here.

options.text: to organise the reasons clearly, one after another
to tell a story in order
options.why: This is a letter giving reasons, not a story.

hints: Find the paragraph with these words.
What comes after each of them?
Why might a reader find this helpful?
items.explanation: Firstly, Secondly and Finally introduce each reason in turn. This makes the reasons easy to follow and more persuasive.

items.prompt: What is the job of the paragraph that begins Some people might say?

options.text: to answer a reason someone might give against the idea
to give the first reason for a refill station
options.why: The reasons are in the paragraph before it.

options.text: to say goodbye politely
options.why: The goodbye is at the end of the letter.

options.text: to tell Mrs Wulan about the 214 bottles
options.why: The bottles are in an earlier paragraph.

hints: Read what some people might say.
Is that a reason for the refill station, or against it?
Then read what the class says straight after However.
items.explanation: This paragraph mentions an argument against the idea, that it costs too much, and then answers it with the cake sale plan.

items.prompt: Under which subheading would you find out what baby Komodo dragons do?

options.text: What they look like
options.why: That part describes their bodies.

options.text: Hunting and eating
options.why: That part is about how the dragons find food.

options.text: Protecting dragons
options.why: That part is about the national park.

options.text: Young dragons

hints: Subheadings tell you what each part is about.
Think of another word for baby animals.
Read each subheading in the report.
items.explanation: The Young dragons section tells us that the babies climb into trees to stay safe.

items.prompt: Why is the report split into sections with subheadings?

options.text: to help readers find information quickly
to make the report look longer
options.why: Subheadings are there to help the reader.

options.text: because each section is a different story
options.why: A report gives facts. It does not tell stories.

options.text: to show the order that things happened in
options.why: This report is organised by topic, not by time.

hints: Imagine you only want to know what Komodo dragons eat.
How would the subheadings help you?
Think about how long it would take without them.
items.explanation: Each subheading names the topic of its section, so readers can go straight to the part they need.

items.prompt: Choose all the features that show this text is a diary.

options.text: a date at the top
Dear Diary
numbered steps
options.why: Numbered steps are a feature of instructions.

options.text: written with I and we
subheadings
options.why: Subheadings are a feature of reports.

hints: A diary is someone's own record of their day.
Look at the start and the end of the text.
Who is telling the events: the writer, or someone else?
items.explanation: A diary has a date, often starts with Dear Diary, and is written in the first person with I and we.

items.prompt: It looked like a giant sleeping dragon breathing out. What does this simile help the reader imagine?

options.text: that a real dragon lived on the mountain
options.why: It is a comparison, not a real dragon.

options.text: that the volcano seemed alive and powerful, with smoke like breath
that the volcano was asleep and could do nothing
options.why: The smoke and the rumbling show it is active.

options.text: that the clouds were shaped like dragons
options.why: The simile is about Mount Bromo, not the clouds.

hints: What does it mean in this sentence?
What does Mount Bromo do in the sentence before?
Why might a puffing volcano remind someone of a dragon?
items.explanation: Bromo puffs out smoke, like a dragon breathing out. The simile makes the volcano seem alive and powerful.

items.prompt: Put the events of the poem in order.
items: The farmers press in the seedlings.
The seedlings grow into a green carpet.
The field turns as gold as honey.
Tin cans keep the sparrows from the grain.
The grain is spread on mats to dry.
The field rests under the rain.
hints: The poem follows the rice field through the year.
Each verse is one stage.
Start with planting time.
items.explanation: The poem moves through the year: planting, growing, ripening, scaring the birds, harvesting and resting.

items.prompt: Why does the poem end with the field becoming a mirror again?

options.text: to show that the farmers bought a new mirror
options.why: The mirror is a comparison for the flooded field.

options.text: because the poet ran out of ideas
options.why: The ending is a careful choice that links back to the start.

options.text: to show that the field is broken
options.why: The field is resting, not broken.

options.text: to show that the year is starting again, like a circle

hints: Read the first line of the poem.
Now read the last line.
What does it mean if a poem ends where it started?
items.explanation: The poem begins and ends with the field as a mirror. This shows that the rice field's year goes round in a cycle.

items.prompt: What is the job of the words in brackets at the start of the play?

options.text: to give the first line that Hana says
options.why: Hana's first line comes after her name.

options.text: to list the things for sale
options.why: There is nothing for sale in the play.

options.text: to tell you where and when the play happens
to tell you how the play ends
options.why: They describe the start, not the end.

hints: Read the first part in brackets.
Does anyone say these words aloud?
What do actors and readers need to know before the play starts?
items.explanation: The opening stage directions set the scene: a beach in Bali, early on a Sunday morning. Nobody says them aloud.

items.prompt: What does the first paragraph of the news report tell you?

options.text: who, what, when and where
what Daniel's favourite job is
options.why: That comes near the end.

options.text: what the class will buy with the money
options.why: That is in the last paragraph.

options.text: what the judges said
options.why: The judges' words come later.

hints: Read only the first paragraph.
Does it say who won and what they won?
Does it also say when and where?
items.explanation: News reports start with the key facts: pupils at Cempaka Primary School (who and where) won first prize (what) last Friday (when).

items.prompt: Why does the reporter include what Mr Hendra said?

options.text: to give the date of the competition
options.why: The date is given elsewhere.

options.text: to show what an expert judge thought of the garden
to explain how to make compost
options.why: He does not explain compost.

options.text: to tell us his favourite vegetable
options.why: He does not mention a favourite vegetable.

hints: Who is Mr Hendra?
Why would a reader care what a judge thinks?
How do the words of real people make a news report feel?
items.explanation: Mr Hendra is a judge, so his words show why the garden won. Quotes from real people make a news report more interesting and believable.
